ch11.note: The Seventy-Two Tenants (Qishi’er jia fangke) is a classic Shanghai huaji comedy, a stage farce, later filmed, about the crowd of tenants packed into one ramshackle lane house, famous for its gallery of city types. The words filling this paragraph — niangyi, afei, biesan, baixiangren and the rest — are Shanghai and Wu-dialect street slang; the author lays them on to fix xiaokai in the same idiom of the 1930s city.

ch11.anchor: his early novel The Bitter Cup
ch11.note: The Bitter Cup (Kubei) was an early novel by Pan Hannian, who first made his name in Shanghai as a left-wing writer and editor before he turned to underground work. The scare-quoted phrases here are the novel’s own romantic-decadent language, which the author quotes with a dry smile.

The Zhongshan suit (after Sun Yat-sen, whose Chinese name was Sun Zhongshan; known in the West as the “Mao suit”) was the plain, semi-military tunic adopted by Chinese revolutionaries and later worn by the Republic’s officials. Because the Kuomintang left and the Communists favored it, wearing one could get a man branded “red.”

The “Left League” is the League of Left-Wing Writers (see the note at Chapter Seven); the “Dramatists’ League” is its sister body, the League of Left-Wing Dramatists. Both were Communist-led cultural fronts of the early 1930s, and Pan Hannian’s Party work in this period ran through them.

ch11.anchor: little Elisa, in The Wild Swans
ch11.note: Hans Christian Andersen’s tale The Wild Swans gives the chapter its title. Its heroine, Elisa, can free her eleven brothers — turned into swans by their stepmother the queen — only by weaving them shirts of nettles, and she may not speak a word until the task is done, on pain of their deaths. Her enforced silence is the author’s figure for the underground worker who can tell no one what he does.

The “CC Clique” was the Kuomintang faction built around the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, which controlled the party’s organization apparatus and, through the Zhongtong (see the note at Chapter One), much of its secret-police and anti-Communist work.

ch11.anchor: Xu Minghong for the Nineteenth Route Army
ch11.note: Xu Minghong (1897–1934) was the Nineteenth Route Army’s secretary-general and a secret Communist, and it was he who negotiated the army’s anti-Japanese accords with Pan Hannian. After the Fujian revolt collapsed he was captured and executed by the Kuomintang in 1934 — the death Liang Shuming mourns below.

The China Weekly Review (Chinese Milei-shi Pinglun-bao, after its American founder Thomas Millard) was Shanghai’s leading English-language weekly, an influential voice on Chinese affairs from 1917 into the 1950s.

ch11.anchor: to resist the outside one must first pacify within
ch11.note: “To resist the outside, first pacify within” (rangwai bi xian annei) was Chiang Kai-shek’s governing slogan of the early 1930s: crush the Communists at home before confronting Japan. It was why he would not back the very resistance to Japan that the Nineteenth Route Army was waging.

ch11.anchor: lending his voice to the "Gongche petition,"
ch11.note: The “Gongche petition” of 1895 — named for the post-carriages that had once carried tribute candidates to the capital — was the mass memorial by examination candidates, led by Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, that protested the treaty ending the war with Japan and demanded reform. It launched the constitutional-reform movement the young Yang Du joined.

Red Flag Weekly (Hongqi Zhoubao) was a central organ of the CCP, published clandestinely in Shanghai from 1931. That Yang Du brushed its masthead is one of the recurring proofs offered, throughout this section, for his secret Party tie.

Qi Baishi (1864–1957), whose original name was Qi Huang, was the most celebrated Chinese painter of the twentieth century, famous above all for his ink studies of shrimp, insects, plants and small creatures.

ch11.anchor: the Annamese patrolmen dare not touch it
ch11.note: The French Concession recruited many of its police in French Indochina; these “Annamese” (Vietnamese) patrolmen answered to the French authorities, so a house under Du Yuesheng’s protection there lay beyond the reach of the Chinese police and the International Settlement’s alike.

Xibaipo, a village in Hebei, was the seat of the CCP Central Committee in 1948–49, on the eve of victory; from it Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai directed the closing campaigns of the civil war and received prospective allies, as here.

ch11.anchor: the editors of the Cihai in Shanghai
ch11.note: The Cihai (“Sea of Words”) is the standard large encyclopedic dictionary of Chinese, compiled and published in Shanghai; an entry in it carries a quasi-official authority, which is why Zhou Enlai wanted Yang Du’s Party membership set down there.

The China Relief Society (Zhongguo Huji Zonghui), founded in 1930, was a Communist-led body that raised money and legal aid for arrested revolutionaries and their families; Song Qingling and Lu Xun were among its public sponsors.

In July 1917 the Qing loyalist general Zhang Xun briefly put the boy emperor Puyi back on the throne in Beijing; the coup collapsed within days. It was this fiasco, Yang Du says, that finally convinced him monarchy was hopeless.
The source prints jiangjun (“generals”) where the sense is plainly Jiang jun, “Chiang’s army”: 150,000 Nationalist troops, not 150,000 generals. Rendered here to the meaning. [—Trans.]

Zhang Yufa (b. 1936) is a leading historian of modern China at Taiwan’s Academia Sinica. The author gives him the last, skeptical word: that Yang Du’s late service to the CCP may have been less a conversion than one more turn of a lifelong gift for playing every side at once.
